one_liner: LLM-agent pipeline that writes a custom C++ executable per SQL query; 2.8x faster than DuckDB on 5 TPC-H queries.
what_it_does: GenDB is not a query engine you link against. It is a Node.js multi-agent pipeline, built on the Claude Agent SDK or the OpenAI Codex SDK, that takes a schema, SQL queries, raw data files and a hardware profile. It outputs a custom columnar storage layout, indexes, and one standalone C++ program per query, which is run as `./qN <gendb_dir> <results_dir> [--param value ...]` and writes CSV. There is no SQL parser or optimizer at runtime. Since March 2026 it extracts parameterized SQL templates, so queries that differ only in literals reuse the same binary; any new query shape needs a fresh LLM generation run.
how_it_is_fast: Five agents (workload analyzer, storage/index designer, query planner, code generator, query optimizer) write code specialized to the exact data statistics and machine. The generated code narrows columns to fit the data (for example, lineitem price stored as int32 cents and discount and quantity as uint8). It picks aggregation by cache fit: a direct per-thread array for Q1's 6 groups, and for Q3's roughly 4M groups a shared open-addressing table with keys and values in separate arrays, updated with lock-free CAS. It also uses zone-map pruning with branchless scans, and query-specific derived structures built at ingest, such as Q9's nibble-packed orderkey-to-year file. Everything runs over mmap'd columns with OpenMP and is compiled with g++ -O3 -march=native. A profiling feedback loop then rewrites slow queries; Q18 went from 12,147 ms to 74 ms when a cache-thrashing hash aggregation was replaced with an index-aware sequential scan.
when_to_use: A fixed set of recurring, templated OLAP queries (scheduled reports, dashboards) where a one-off generation run pays for itself. The demo paper puts it at about $14 and 91 minutes for 5 TPC-H queries, and $23 and 140 minutes for 6 SEC-EDGAR queries, with Sonnet 4.6.
Read-mostly analytical data that fits in RAM on a many-core Linux x86-64 server, where hot latency in the tens of milliseconds at the ~10 GB scale matters.
A hybrid setup, which the authors themselves recommend: DuckDB or Umbra keep serving ad-hoc SQL while the hottest query templates are routed to GenDB binaries.

A readable starting point for hand-tuning a critical query. The generated C++ is plain, self-contained code, and the repo's language comparison got a further 1.30x on TPC-H with a human-directed refinement pass.
Research on LLM-synthesized query processing: the full pipeline is open, and ablation, model-comparison and iteration-history data are checked in.
when_not_to_use: Ad-hoc or exploratory SQL. Every new query shape needs an LLM generation run (minutes to hours, and paid API use), and nothing at runtime can answer a query that was not generated in advance.

Data that changes or grows. Storage is a custom format produced by a generated ingest program, and the binaries hard-code SF10 key ranges and thread counts. Inserts, updates and transactions are not documented.

Workloads that need guaranteed correct answers. Validation only matches results against DuckDB ground truth, plus fuzzing across template parameters in the newer version, and the authors say this does not prove semantic equivalence. The paper documents LLM bugs: dropped DECIMAL scale divisions that gave wrong results, and open-addressing tables with no resize or probe bound that looped forever.

Non-Linux, non-x86 or mixed hardware fleets. The pipeline reads /proc/cpuinfo, lscpu and lsblk, the binaries are built with -march=native, and every published number comes from one 2x Xeon Gold 5218 server.

Anything production-critical. Results vary a lot between generation runs: a later Sonnet 4.6 run got 285 ms on TPC-H (paper: 214 ms) and 830 ms on SEC-EDGAR (paper: 328 ms). The README warns that Sonnet 4.6 agents now hang, and baselines were compared on only 5 TPC-H queries and 6 SEC-EDGAR queries.

integration.dependencies: Generator: Node.js 18+ with npm packages @anthropic-ai/claude-agent-sdk, @anthropic-ai/claude-code, @openai/codex-sdk and openai; an Anthropic or OpenAI API key or subscription; Python 3 for result comparison and benchmarks; DuckDB for ground truth. Generated binaries: g++ with OpenMP, pthreads and POSIX mmap only.
integration.min_toolchain: C++17 (g++ -O3 -march=native -std=c++17 -fopenmp); the GCC version is not documented; Node.js 18+
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 in practice (tested only on 2x Xeon Gold 5218 with AVX-512 and 64 threads). The hardware probe recognizes NEON, but aarch64 is not documented or tested.
integration.thread_safety: Not applicable in the usual sense. Each query is a separate process that uses all cores through OpenMP (one run hard-codes N_THREADS = 64), and the orchestrator runs one query at a time while timing. Running several concurrently is not documented.

gotchas: The query times are not measured the same way for GenDB and the baselines. GenDB's number is the binary's own [TIMING] total minus its output phase. DuckDB, Umbra and the others are timed from the Python client and include fetchall(). Work done at ingest time (indexes, derived files like Q9's orderkey-to-year nibble file) is not counted at all.

Generated code is sized for the data it was generated against. Examples: Q9 declares part_bitset[2000001] and suppkey_nk[100001] with N_THREADS = 64, and the latest Q3 uses BITMAP_MAX = 1500001, all SF10 key ranges. A larger dataset or a different machine needs regeneration; the orchestrator re-benchmarks on a hardware-fingerprint change.

Bug in the shared helper src/gendb/utils/hash_utils.h: when CompactHashMap::operator[] displaces an entry (Robin Hood), it overwrites `key` with the displaced key before its final lookup. It then returns the displaced key's value slot, so `m[k] += v` can update the wrong group. The generated files checked use find() plus insert(), which avoids this path.

The checked-in runs cannot execute from a fresh clone. The storage folders (12 GB for TPC-H, 3.3 GB for SEC-EDGAR) must be downloaded from Google Drive. The stable paper version is on branch arxiv-03-02-2026, and main has since moved to template-native generation.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick GenDB over Bespoke OLAP (also LLM-synthesized per workload, headline numbers single-threaded) and JetStream (generates accelerators that sit beside an existing DBMS) when you want standalone, multi-threaded C++ executables per query template from an Apache-2.0 pipeline that can use either Claude or Codex agents. Pick Umbra, Sirius or plain DuckDB whenever you need a real SQL engine that handles arbitrary queries without a generation step.
verified_claims_summary: On the paper's setup (2x Xeon Gold 5218, 64 threads, 384 GB RAM, hot in-memory runs, mean of 3 runs after a warm-up), Sonnet 4.6-generated C++ built with g++ -O3 -march=native -fopenmp ran 5 TPC-H SF10 queries in 214 ms. That compares with 594 ms for DuckDB v1.4.4 and 590 ms for Umbra (2.8x). Per query versus DuckDB: Q1 40 vs 84 ms, Q3 55 vs 83, Q6 14 vs 19, Q9 38 vs 231, Q18 68 vs 177. On SEC-EDGAR (6 queries) it took 328 ms, versus 1,549 ms for DuckDB and 1,280 ms for Umbra. The later template-native version (VLDB 2026 demo paper) reports smaller gains: 249 ms, 2.4x versus DuckDB and 2.7x versus Umbra on TPC-H, and 403 ms, 3.8x versus DuckDB on SEC-EDGAR.
status_note: A Cornell research prototype (arXiv 2603.02081 plus a VLDB 2026 demo paper), licensed Apache-2.0 although package.json still says ISC, with 75 stars. The last code change was 2026-03-27 and the 2026-06-08 commit only touched the README, so 'active' is generous. You can run the generator if you have LLM API access and a Linux server; the reusable output is generated C++ per query, not a library to vendor.
